title: Automate a chore with codex exec
goal: You will use Codex non-interactively to replace a configuration key across a project and verify every resulting edit.
prerequisites: A Git-tracked project with a repeated config key
A clean working tree or a saved backup

steps.action: Change into the project directory you want Codex to modify.
steps.why: Codex uses the selected directory as the project workspace.
steps.checkpoint: The prompt displays your project path.
hint_levels: Check which folder the prompt currently shows.
Use Set-Location with the full path to your project.
Type Set-Location "C:\path\to\project" and press Enter.

steps.action: Confirm that the working tree is clean by running git status --short.
steps.where: Windows Terminal PowerShell prompt inside the project directory.
steps.why: A clean baseline makes Codex's edits easy to isolate and undo.
steps.checkpoint: The command returns no file entries.
hint_levels: Ask Git for its compact status view.
The --short option lists only changed and untracked files.
Type git status --short and press Enter.

steps.action: Locate every current occurrence by running rg -n "OLD_CONFIG_KEY" .
steps.where: Windows Terminal PowerShell prompt inside the project directory.
steps.why: The search establishes the expected scope before automation changes anything.
steps.checkpoint: The terminal lists matching file paths, line numbers, and text.
hint_levels: Search recursively before editing.
Replace OLD_CONFIG_KEY with the exact existing key while keeping the quotes.
Type rg -n "OLD_CONFIG_KEY" . and press Enter.

steps.action: Run codex exec --sandbox workspace-write "Replace OLD_CONFIG_KEY with NEW_CONFIG_KEY everywhere it represents the project configuration key, preserve formatting, do not alter generated or dependency files, and report the files changed."
steps.where: Windows Terminal PowerShell prompt inside the project directory.
steps.why: This invokes Codex non-interactively with permission limited to writing inside the workspace.
steps.checkpoint: The command finishes without an interactive prompt and prints a summary of changed files.
hint_levels: Use the Codex subcommand intended for scripted runs.
Give exec workspace-write access and describe both the old and new key precisely.
Paste the command, replace both placeholder keys, and press Enter.

steps.action: Review the resulting patch by running git diff -- .
steps.where: Windows Terminal PowerShell prompt inside the project directory.
steps.why: The diff reveals every modification before you accept the automated work.
steps.checkpoint: The terminal shows only the intended key replacements in the expected files.
hint_levels: Inspect Git's unstaged changes.
Limit the diff to the current project path.
Type git diff -- . and press Enter.

steps.action: Search again for the old key by running rg -n "OLD_CONFIG_KEY" .
steps.where: Windows Terminal PowerShell prompt inside the project directory.
steps.why: A second search detects missed references that the automation should have handled.
steps.checkpoint: The terminal shows no relevant occurrences of the old key.
hint_levels: Repeat the search that established your baseline.
Use the old key, not the replacement key, in the pattern.
Type rg -n "OLD_CONFIG_KEY" . and press Enter.

steps.action: Run the project's existing validation command.
steps.where: Windows Terminal PowerShell prompt at the project root, using the command defined by the project's package or build configuration.
steps.why: Automated text changes still need the project's normal checks.
steps.checkpoint: The terminal displays a successful test, lint, or validation result with no failing checks.
hint_levels: Use the same check the project normally runs before a commit.
Look in package.json, Makefile, or the build configuration for the validation script.
Run the project's command, such as npm test, dotnet test, or pytest, and press Enter.

steps.action: Inspect the final changed-file list by running git status --short.
steps.where: Windows Terminal PowerShell prompt inside the project directory.
steps.why: The final status confirms the exact scope of the completed chore.
steps.checkpoint: Only the files expected from the config-key update appear as modified.
hint_levels: Finish with Git's compact summary.
Compare this list with the files Codex reported and the earlier search results.
Type git status --short and press Enter.
